en.title: Propositions and phrases
en.summary: A first map of English grammar: sentences, clauses, phrases and the ten classes of words.

paragraphs: Grammar is the set of rules that tells you how words fit together. This lesson gives you a map. First you will see what a sentence is, and what grammar books call a proposition. Then you will meet the ten classes of words and the ideas, such as number and tense, that come back again and again. The next lessons in this chapter look at each class in detail.

A **sentence** is a group of words that gives a complete message. It starts with a capital letter and ends with a full stop, a question mark or an exclamation mark. Every sentence has a **subject**, which is who or what the sentence is about, and a **predicate**, which is what we say about the subject.

blocks.html:
PartWhat it isExample
Subjectwho or what the sentence is aboutMy sister works in a bank.
Predicatewhat we say about the subjectMy sister works in a bank.
Clausea group of words with its own subject and verbShe works because she likes numbers.
Phrasea group of words without its own subject and verbin a bank, my younger sister

paragraphs: In Romanian, French and Italian the usual word for a clause looks like proposition. In English we usually say clause. The word proposition stays in English for a statement that can be true or false, such as in logic.
A sentence can do four jobs. It can give information, ask for it, give an order or show a strong feeling.

blocks.html:
KindIts jobExample
Statementgives informationThe train leaves at nine.
Questionasks for informationDoes the train leave at nine?
Commandtells someone to do somethingWait here, please.
Exclamationshows a strong feelingWhat a beautiful day!

paragraphs: Sentences also differ in how many clauses they have. A simple sentence has one clause. A compound sentence joins two clauses of equal weight. A complex sentence has a main clause and a clause that depends on it.

items: **Simple sentence, one clause:** The bus is late.
**Compound sentence, two equal clauses:** The bus is late, but I can wait.
**Complex sentence, a main clause and a dependent clause:** I can wait because the bus is always late.

paragraphs: Every English word belongs to a class, and the class tells you what the word can do in a sentence. Some grammar books put articles and numerals under one name, determiners. The list of ten is the traditional one and it works well for learners.

blocks.html:
ClassWhat it doesExamples
Nounnames a person, place, thing or ideateacher, London, happiness
Pronounstands in place of a nounshe, them, this
Articleshows whether a noun is known or newthe, a, an
Adjectivedescribes a nounsmall, red, interesting
Verbshows an action, a state or an eventrun, be, seem
Adverbtells how, when, where or how muchquickly, now, very
Prepositionlinks a noun to the rest of the sentencein, on, with
Conjunctionjoins words, phrases and clausesand, but, because
Numeraltells a number or an orderthree, second
Interjectionshows a sudden feelingoh, wow, ouch

paragraphs: One word can belong to two classes. In **a light bag** the word light is an adjective, and in **turn on the light** it is a noun. Always ask what the word does in this sentence.
These ideas appear in almost every grammar lesson. English uses some of them a lot and others hardly at all, which is useful to know if your own language is very different.

blocks.html:
IdeaThe question it answersIn English
Numberone, or more than one?book, books
Gendermasculine, feminine or neuter?only in pronouns: he, she, it
Casewhat job does the word do?only in pronouns and the 's ending: I, me, my
Personwho speaks, who is spoken to, who is spoken about?I, you, he
Tensewhen does it happen?walk, walked, will walk
Moodis it a fact, a wish or an order?She is here. Be quiet!
Voicedoes the subject act or receive the action?The cook made the soup. The soup was made by the cook.
Aspectis the action finished or in progress?I wrote. I was writing.
Agreementwhich words must match?This book is new. These books are new.

paragraphs: English sentences usually follow the order subject, verb, object. In **The cat chased the mouse** the cat is the subject, chased is the verb and the mouse is the object. English has almost no case endings, so the order of the words tells you who did what. **The mouse chased the cat** has the same words but a different meaning.

The next lessons take the word classes one by one: nouns, articles, adjectives, pronouns, numerals, verbs, adverbs, prepositions and conjunctions. After that you will meet the same ideas inside real texts, in the chapters about people, home, town and work. Each of those texts carries short grammar notes that point back to the lesson on the topic.
